x.t: More than 100,000 people move to safety before storm Akvan
b: Helpers in Odisha have now moved more than 100,000 people to safety. They are staying in [[shelter|shelters]], safe buildings for storms.
The [[cyclone|storm]] Akvan is likely to reach land by about noon on Friday. This is called [[landfall|landfall]]. Rescue teams are ready to help.
Rain has begun in Odisha. The sea gets rough, so fishermen are told not to go out. Tourists cannot visit some beaches.

o.t: More than one lakh people moved to safety as Akvan nears Odisha
b: More than one lakh (100,000) people have been moved to safety in Odisha ahead of [[cyclone|Cyclone]] Akvan. On Thursday 19 November, senior Odisha official Anu Garg said 1,05,304 people were in 1,224 [[shelter|shelters]]. Evacuation, moving people away from danger, was still going on.

The [[imd|IMD]], India's weather office, expects Akvan to make [[landfall|landfall]] near Gopalpur in Ganjam district by about noon on Friday 20 November. Landfall is when the centre of a cyclone crosses from the sea onto land. Winds of 90 to 100 kilometres an hour are expected. Rain has begun in Odisha and should get heavier.

Sixty Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force teams and 14 [[ndrf|NDRF]] teams are ready to help. The sea gets rough near a cyclone, so fishermen are told not to go out. Tourists are kept away from the beaches of Gopalpur and Puri, and from Satapada and Chilika.

stories.think: Why do you think helpers move people to shelters before a storm arrives, and not after it starts?

quiz.q: How many people had Odisha moved to safety by Thursday?

x.t: Leaders of China, the US and Russia meet together for the first time
b: The leaders of China, the United States and Russia met in China on Thursday. It was the first time all three met together.
Afterwards, a [[declaration|declaration]] was shared in their names. This is a written message about what they plan to do. It is not a law.
It says they want to help the [[united-nations|United Nations]] work better. It also says they will keep talking.

o.t: Leaders of China, the US and Russia meet; peace declaration released
b: Presidents Xi Jinping of China, Donald Trump of the United States and Vladimir Putin of Russia met together for the first time on Thursday 19 November, in Shenzhen, China. They met alongside the [[apec|APEC]] summit, the yearly meeting of Asia-Pacific economies.

China's government-run news outlets published a peace [[declaration|declaration]] in the names of the three leaders. A declaration is a written statement of what leaders say they intend to do. It is not a law or a treaty, a formal agreement between countries, so it does not force anyone to act. The declaration says a nuclear war can never be won and must never be fought.

It also says the three will hold talks on reducing nuclear risks, and are committed to reforming the [[united-nations|United Nations]] so it can deal better with global problems. All three have permanent seats on its Security Council.

stories.think: Why might it matter that leaders write down what they intend to do, even when it is not a law?

quiz.q: What is a declaration, as explained in the story?
a: A law that everyone must obey
A written statement of what leaders say they intend to do
A vote by all the world's people
A new flag for the United Nations

x.t: A big win and a finals place for Indian badminton
b: India's Rakshitha Ramraj won a big [[badminton|badminton]] match on Thursday. She beat a former Olympic champion from China. Now she is in the Hong Kong Open's last eight.

[[lakshya|Lakshya Sen]] has a place in the [[world-tour-finals|World Tour Finals]]. Only the year's top eight in each event can play. Another Indian, Kidambi Srikanth, helped by beating the player chasing Lakshya's place.
PV Sindhu will play there too, in China in December.

o.t: Rakshitha Ramraj wins in Hong Kong as Lakshya Sen makes season finals
b: India's Rakshitha Ramraj beat Chen Yu Fei of China, a former Olympic champion, 21-18, 24-22 at the Hong Kong Open on Thursday 19 November. The win took her into the [[quarter-final|quarter-finals]], the round for the last eight players.

[[lakshya|Lakshya Sen]] has qualified for the [[bwf|BWF]] [[world-tour-finals|World Tour Finals]], the last big event of the [[badminton|badminton]] season. Only the top eight players or pairs in each event qualify. Lakshya's place was sealed on Wednesday 18 November, when another Indian, Kidambi Srikanth, beat Japan's Koki Watanabe 21-16, 16-21, 21-9. Watanabe was the player chasing Lakshya's place, so his defeat made Lakshya's place safe.
PV Sindhu has also qualified, in women's singles. The World Tour Finals will be held in Hangzhou, China, from 9 to 13 December. Before then, Rakshitha plays on in the Hong Kong quarter-finals.

stories.think: Kidambi Srikanth was playing his own match, but his win also helped Lakshya Sen. Can you think of a time when something someone did helped others too?

quiz.q: How many players or pairs in each event qualify for the World Tour Finals?

x.t: Data centres set to give off more carbon, report says
b: Chatbots, videos and games run on computers in big buildings called [[data-centre|data centres]]. They need lots of electricity.
An energy group called the [[iea|IEA]] has a new report. It says data centres' [[carbon-emissions|carbon gases]] are set to rise by 70% by 2030.
These gases come from burning coal and gas for electricity. They make the planet warmer. Most of the growth in data centres is expected to be for [[ai|AI]].

o.t: Data centre carbon emissions set to rise 70% by 2030, says IEA
b: Chatbots, online videos and online games run on computers in large buildings called [[data-centre|data centres]], which need electricity. The [[iea|International Energy Agency]] (IEA), which studies energy, has published its yearly report.

It says [[carbon-emissions|carbon emissions]] from data centres are set to rise by 70% by 2030. Carbon emissions are gases such as carbon dioxide, released when fuels like coal and gas burn. They trap heat and warm the planet. This rise comes from electricity made in gas and coal power plants. The IEA expects about three-quarters of the growth in data centres to be for [[ai|artificial intelligence]] (AI), computer programs that can learn and make choices.

The IEA used [[satellite|satellite]] pictures to track 93 large AI data centres. It found that data centre capacity, or how much computing and power they can handle, grew about ten times in two years. So where data centres get their electricity matters.

stories.think: Chatbots, videos and games all use electricity in data centres. Should people keep this in mind when they go online? Why or why not?

quiz.q: By how much does the IEA say data centre carbon emissions are set to rise by 2030?

x.t: Scientists find an insect that may be a new kind
b: Scientists went to [[navarino-island|Navarino Island]] in Chile. They were looking for an insect called the Patagonian dragon. They found a different insect.
It is a [[stonefly|stonefly]]. It does not match any known [[species|species]], or kind of living thing. So it may be a new species.
It was found beside a [[glacier|glacier]] that is shrinking. Nobody knows yet if it lives anywhere else. Scientists need to study it more.

o.t: Stonefly found beside a shrinking glacier may be a new species
b: Scientists in Chile have found a [[stonefly|stonefly]], a kind of insect, that may be a new [[species|species]]. The team, led by Javier Rendoll-Carcamo and including scientists from the University of Magallanes, found it on [[navarino-island|Navarino Island]], in the far south of Chilean [[patagonia|Patagonia]]. They had gone looking for a different insect, the Patagonian dragon.

A species is one kind of living thing. To check whether something is new, scientists compare it with species that have already been described, or named. The researchers could not match this stonefly to any described species, so it may be new, but more study is needed. Their findings were published in the scientific journal Ecology.
The insect was found about 780 metres above sea level, beside the remains of a [[glacier|glacier]] that is retreating, or shrinking. Scientists do not yet know whether it lives only there.

stories.think: Why do you think scientists still search for new kinds of living things, even tiny insects?

quiz.q: Which insect was the team looking for when they found the stonefly?

x.t: India's big film festival opens in Goa on Friday
b: A big [[film-festival|film festival]] opens in [[goa|Goa]] on Friday. It is the International Film Festival of India. It runs until Saturday 28 November.
At a film festival, lots of films are shown to audiences. This year there are films from 86 countries.
The [[theme|theme]] is "Stories Without Borders". It means stories can be shared between countries. For the first time, there is a group of five animated films.

o.t: 57th International Film Festival of India opens in Goa on Friday
b: The 57th International Film Festival of India runs in [[goa|Goa]] from Friday 20 November to Saturday 28 November. A [[film-festival|film festival]] is an event where many films are shown, and some are judged, over several days. This year's [[theme|theme]], or main idea, is "Stories Without Borders": stories can be shared across the borders between countries.

The festival includes more than 150 films from other countries. In all, its films come from 86 countries. Spain is the Country of Honour and Russia is the Partner Country. The opening film is "Fatherland", directed by Pawel Pawlikowski, who won Best Director at the [[cannes|Cannes Film Festival]].

The festival director is film-maker Ashutosh Gowariker. Aanand L Rai chairs the [[jury|jury]], the panel of judges, for the International Competition. For the first time, the festival has a section just for animated films, with five films.

stories.think: If you could choose one film to show children in another country, what would you want it to be about?

quiz.q: What is the theme of this year's festival?

x.t: South Korea's sales to other countries pass 1 trillion dollars
b: South Korea sells lots of goods to other countries. These sales are called [[exports|exports]]. On Thursday, this year's exports passed one [[trillion|trillion]] dollars.
It is a first for South Korea. Only three countries got there before: the United States, Germany and China.
More than 4 in every 10 dollars came from [[semiconductor|computer chips]]. These tiny parts help phones and computers work. The count goes on until December ends.

o.t: South Korea's exports pass 1 trillion dollars for the first time
b: South Korea's [[exports|exports]] for 2026 passed 1 [[trillion|trillion]] US dollars shortly after 2 pm Korean time on Thursday 19 November, [[trade-ministry|the country's trade ministry]] said. Exports are goods that a country sells to buyers in other countries. A trillion is a million million. It is the first time South Korea has reached this mark.
South Korea is only the fourth country to sell 1 trillion dollars of goods abroad in a single year. The other three are the United States, Germany and China.

One product did much of the work: [[semiconductor|semiconductors]], or computer chips, the tiny parts that help phones, computers and many other machines work. Chips made up more than 40% of South Korea's exports. From January to October 2026, the country sold 396.8 billion dollars of chips abroad. The yearly total will keep growing until the end of December.

stories.think: Is it helpful, risky or a bit of both for a country to sell a lot of one product? Why?

quiz.q: Which product made up more than 40% of South Korea's exports?

x.t: China launches a new satellite into space
b: China sent a new [[satellite|satellite]] into space on Thursday. It is called Shijian-24. Reports did not say what it will do.
A big [[rocket|rocket]] carried it up from a launch site in north China. Rockets push upward very fast to reach space.
The launch went well. Shijian-24 is now in its planned [[orbit|orbit]]. That is its path around Earth.

o.t: China launches Shijian-24, a new satellite
b: China launched a new [[satellite|satellite]] called Shijian-24 at 6.51 am Beijing time on Thursday 19 November. Reports did not say what this satellite will do.

It was carried by a Long March-2D [[rocket|rocket]] from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province, north China. A rocket burns fuel and pushes hot gas out behind it, which drives it upward fast enough to carry a satellite into space. This was the 678th flight by a rocket from the Long March family.

The launch was described as a success: Shijian-24 entered its planned [[orbit|orbit]], the path it follows around Earth. A satellite stays in orbit because it moves sideways very fast while Earth's gravity keeps pulling on it, so it keeps curving around the planet. Shijian-24 is now travelling along that path.

stories.think: Satellites help with jobs such as taking pictures and studying weather. Which satellite job do you think helps people most, and why?

quiz.q: Which rocket carried Shijian-24 into space?

cyclone: A big storm that forms over the sea, with strong winds and rain.
A large storm that forms over the sea, with strong winds and heavy rain. India's weather office uses names such as severe cyclonic storm for stronger levels.
shelter: A safe building where people can stay during a storm.
A safe building where people can stay away from danger. Before Akvan, more than one lakh people in Odisha moved into 1,224 cyclone and flood shelters.
landfall: When the middle of a big storm moves from the sea onto land.
The moment when the centre of a cyclone crosses from the sea onto land. Akvan is expected to make landfall in Odisha by about noon on Friday 20 November.
imd: India's weather office. It watches storms and gives forecasts.
The India Meteorological Department, India's weather office. It tracks storms and gives forecasts and alerts.
ndrf: India's national team of trained rescue helpers.
The National Disaster Response Force, India's national force of trained rescue teams. Fourteen NDRF teams are ready in Odisha for Akvan.
declaration: A written message about what leaders plan to do. It is not a law.
A written statement of what leaders say they intend to do. It is not a law or a treaty, so it does not force anyone to act.
apec: A yearly meeting of countries from Asia and around the Pacific Ocean.
The yearly summit, or top-level meeting, of Asia-Pacific economies. In 2026 it was held in Shenzhen, China.
united-nations: A group where nearly all the world's countries work together.
An organisation of nearly every country in the world, set up to keep peace and work on shared problems. China, Russia and the United States all have permanent seats on its Security Council.
data-centre: A big building full of computers that run apps, videos and games.
A large building full of computers that store information and run online services such as chatbots, videos and games. Data centres need a lot of electricity.
iea: A group that studies energy around the world.
The International Energy Agency, an international organisation that studies energy. It publishes a report on world energy every year.
carbon-emissions: Gases, such as carbon dioxide, that go into the air when coal or gas is burned. They make the planet warmer.
Carbon dioxide and similar gases released into the air, for example when coal or gas is burned to make electricity. These gases trap heat and warm the planet.
ai: Artificial intelligence: computer programs that can learn and make choices.
Artificial intelligence: the ability of computers and other machines to do things thought to need intelligence, such as understanding spoken language or making decisions.
satellite: A machine sent into space that travels round and round Earth.
A machine sent into orbit around Earth or another body. Satellites are used for jobs such as communication, taking pictures and studying weather.
navarino-island: An island in the far south of Chile.
An island in the far south of Chilean Patagonia, in South America.
stonefly: A kind of insect. There are many different kinds of stoneflies.
A kind of insect. Scientists group stoneflies together in an insect order called Plecoptera.
species: One kind of living thing, such as a tiger or a house sparrow.
One kind of living thing. When scientists describe a new species, they give it an official name.
patagonia: A large area in the far south of South America.
A large region in the far south of South America. Part of it is in Chile.
glacier: A huge mass of ice on land that moves very slowly.
A large mass of ice on land that moves very slowly. When it melts faster than new snow builds it up, it retreats, or shrinks.
film-festival: A big event where lots of films are shown to audiences.
An event, often lasting several days, where many films are shown to audiences and some compete for prizes.
goa: A state in India, by the sea.
A small state on the west coast of India.
theme: The main idea or subject that links the parts of something, such as the films at a festival.
cannes: A famous film festival held every year in Cannes, a town in France.
One of the world's best-known film festivals, held every year in the town of Cannes in France. Its prizes include Best Director.
jury: A group of people who choose the winner of a contest.
A group of people chosen to judge a competition and decide who wins.
rocket: A machine that shoots up into the sky by pushing hot gas out behind it.
A vehicle that burns fuel and pushes hot gas out behind it, which drives it forward very fast. Rockets carry satellites and spacecraft into space.
orbit: The path something follows as it goes round and round a planet, moon or star.
The curved path an object follows around a planet, moon or star, held there by gravity.
exports: Things a country sells to other countries.
Goods that one country sells to buyers in other countries.
trillion: A huge number: a million million.
A million million, written as 1 followed by 12 zeros. One trillion is the same as 1,000 billion.
semiconductor: A computer chip: a tiny part that helps phones and computers work.
A material used to make computer chips. In trade news the word usually means the chips themselves, which help phones, computers and many other machines work.
trade-ministry: The part of a government that looks after buying and selling with other countries.
The government department that deals with trade, the buying and selling of goods, including with other countries. South Korea's trade ministry announced the 1 trillion dollar mark.
badminton: A game where players hit a feathered shuttle over a high net with rackets.
A racket sport in which players hit a shuttlecock back and forth over a high net. A point is won when the shuttlecock lands on the other side's court.
quarter-final: The round of a contest when eight players are left.
The round of a knockout tournament played by the last eight players or teams. The winners go on to the semi-finals.
world-tour-finals: The last big badminton contest of the year. Only the top eight in each event play.
The BWF World Tour Finals, the last big event of the badminton season. Only the top eight players or pairs in each event qualify. In 2026 it is in Hangzhou, China, from 9 to 13 December.
lakshya: An Indian badminton player. He has qualified for the 2026 BWF World Tour Finals.
bwf: The group that runs badminton around the world.
The Badminton World Federation, the organisation that governs badminton around the world and runs its top international tournaments.
jpl: A NASA centre in California. The Voyager 1 mission is run from there.
A NASA laboratory in California. The Voyager mission is run from there.
light-day: How far light travels in one whole day. It is a very long way.
A unit of distance: how far light travels in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometres.
deep-space-network: NASA's big antennas that keep track of faraway spacecraft.
NASA's network of giant radio antennas, with sites in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. It keeps track of Voyager 1.
interstellar: The space between the stars. Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to enter it, in 2012.
fossil: The remains or mark of an animal or plant that lived long ago.
The remains or trace of an animal or plant that lived long ago.

in-akvan.ctx: Akvan is a severe cyclonic storm, and the IMD expects it to cross the coast between Narsapur in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Odisha. In West Bengal, rain is forecast for Kolkata and south Bengal, and fishermen there have been told to stay off the sea. In Bangladesh, ships between Cox's Bazar and St Martin's Island stopped on Thursday because the sea is rough, so tourists are waiting on the island until the ships restart.
in-akvan.ask: Officials close beaches and keep boats in harbour days before a cyclone arrives. Should they act this early, even if a storm turns out weaker than expected, or wait until forecasts are more certain so daily life and work stop for less time?

g-ai-datacentres.ctx: Companies that build data centres are the biggest business buyers of green electricity in the world. Even so, their fast growth is also pushing up demand for fossil fuels. When the 93 giant AI centres are finished, together they will need about 50 gigawatts of power.
g-ai-datacentres.ask: AI tools are useful to many people, but the data centres that run them use a lot of electricity. Should new AI data centres only be built where there is cleaner electricity, even if that slows AI down, or should they be allowed to grow quickly because of what AI can do?

g-stonefly.ctx: The stonefly belongs to a family of stoneflies called Gripopterygidae, in the insect order Plecoptera. The new stonefly was found beside the glacier's remains, and scientists say it could be at risk if the glacier keeps shrinking.
g-stonefly.ask: This stonefly was found beside a glacier that is shrinking. Some people think scientists should hurry to find and name species in places that are changing fast. Others think slow, careful study matters more, even if it takes years. Which matters more?

bigStory.t: How far is one light-day from home?
bigStory.sub: Voyager 1, launched in 1977, reaches one light-day from Earth on Wednesday

x.why: A spacecraft that left Earth in 1977 is still travelling. This week it will be so far away that light needs a whole day to reach it.

o.why: A spacecraft launched in 1977 is still travelling, and its team on Earth still talks to it. This week it reaches a distance so great that a radio signal, moving at the speed of light, needs 24 hours to get there.

facts: about one light-day: how far light travels in 24 hours
how long a radio signal from Earth now takes to reach it
the day NASA says it reaches one light-day

days.o: NASA launched Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977. It flew past Jupiter in 1979 and Saturn in 1980, and in 1990 it took a picture of Earth known as the Pale Blue Dot. In 2012 it entered interstellar space, the space between the stars. It is run from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California.
days.x: Voyager 1 is a spacecraft. It left Earth in 1977. It flew past the planets Jupiter and Saturn. In 1990 it took a picture of Earth from very far away.

days.o: A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, about 25.9 billion kilometres. Light reaches the Moon in about 1.3 seconds, and sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. After sunset today, Tuesday 17 November, NASA invites people to flash VGR, Voyager's three-letter call sign, in Morse code towards the sky with a torch.
days.x: A light-day is how far light travels in one day. Sunlight reaches us in about 8 minutes. After sunset today, people can flash a torch for Voyager. Ask a grown-up to help.

days.o: NASA worked out that Voyager 1 would reach one light-day from Earth on Wednesday 18 November. No spacecraft has travelled this far before. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach it, and its reply takes another day to come back. Voyager 2 is expected to reach one light-day in 2035.
days.x: On Wednesday, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. No spacecraft has gone this far before. A message now takes about a day to get there.

days.o: NASA talks to Voyager 1 by radio through its Deep Space Network, a set of giant radio antennas at three sites: Goldstone in California, near Madrid in Spain and near Canberra in Australia. The sites are placed around the world so that they can keep in contact with a spacecraft as Earth turns. Each site has one antenna that is 70 metres across. A radio signal now takes about 24 hours to reach Voyager 1, and its reply takes another 24 hours to come back, so a message and its answer make a two-day round trip.
days.x: NASA talks to Voyager 1 with radio signals. It uses giant radio antennas in California, Spain and Australia. A message takes about a day to reach Voyager 1. The reply takes another day to come back.

days.lock: Friday: the week in one page, and where Voyager 1 goes from here.

days.name: World Toilet Day
days.what: World Toilet Day is marked on 19 November. It was started in 2001 by the World Toilet Organization and became an official United Nations day in 2013.

days.name: World Heritage Week begins
days.what: In India, World Heritage Week is observed from 19 to 25 November. The Archaeological Survey of India marks it.

born.name: Indira Gandhi
born.what: Born in Allahabad, India. She was the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister. She was prime minister of India from 1966 to 1977 and again from 1980 to 1984.

born.name: José Raúl Capablanca
born.what: A chess player born in Havana, Cuba. He learned chess at the age of four. He became world chess champion in 1921 and held the title until 1927.

today.week: World Children's Day is on Friday 20 November.

learn.subject: Science
learn.link: From this week's Big Story: talking to Voyager 1

b: Radio waves are a kind of wave that carries messages from place to place.
They are very fast. They travel as fast as light. They can even cross empty space.
Radio and television use radio waves. So do many wireless gadgets, and the people who talk to spacecraft.
x.remember: Radio waves travel as fast as light and can cross empty space.
x.q: Can radio waves cross empty space?

b: Radio waves are a type of electromagnetic wave. Light is an electromagnetic wave too. Radio waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres every second, and they can travel through empty space.
Radio and television programmes are sent using radio waves, and many modern wireless devices use them to send information. So does the team that talks to Voyager 1.

The scientist James Clerk Maxwell predicted electromagnetic waves in the 1860s. In the late 1880s, the German physicist Heinrich Hertz showed that they exist. The hertz, a unit used to measure the frequency of waves, is named after him.
o.remember: Radio waves are electromagnetic waves. They travel at the speed of light and can cross empty space.
o.q: Who showed in the late 1880s that radio waves exist?

backThen.t: Pelé scores the 1,000th goal of his career
backThen.o: On 19 November 1969, the Brazilian footballer Pelé scored the 1,000th goal of his career. He was playing for his club, Santos, against Vasco da Gama at the Maracanã stadium in Rio de Janeiro. The goal was a penalty kick, scored in the 78th minute. Reporters and photographers ran onto the pitch.
backThen.x: On this day in 1969, the footballer Pelé scored his 1,000th goal. He scored it from a penalty kick at a stadium in Brazil. Reporters and photographers ran onto the pitch.
backThen.why: Pelé dedicated the goal to the children of Brazil. This Friday, 20 November, is World Children's Day.

hiddenWords.o: Fossil comes from the Latin word fossilis, which means dug up. It comes from fodere, the Latin word for to dig.
The word cyclone was made up in 1848 by Henry Piddington, from Greek words meaning circle and moving in a circle.
